title: No place for the tiger
hook: one who knows how to live meets no tiger, for there's no place in him for its claws (Tao Te Ching 50)

segments.voice: Yesterday, no fixed mind: the sage who is good even to those who are not good. Your line was good to all. Who tested that line for you yesterday? Day one thousand one hundred twelve.

A traveler is crossing wild country. There are rhinoceroses in the long grass, tigers in the hills, and somewhere up ahead, soldiers. A sensible traveler would plan a route around all of it. Chapter fifty of the Tao Te Ching describes someone who walks straight through and comes out untouched. The odd part is the explanation. The chapter never says the tiger is gone, or tame, or asleep. It says the tiger can't find anywhere on this person to hold on. Today, a traveler with no place for the claws.
screen: `RHINOCEROS, TIGER, SOLDIERS.` → `THE TRAVELER WALKS THROUGH.` → `NOWHERE TO HOLD ON.`

segments.voice: First, where the chapter starts. Not with tigers, but with life and death. People come out into life and go back into death, it says, and some of them hurry toward death by straining too hard to keep living. Clutching at life, in this chapter, is its own danger. Second, the traveler. In James Legge's translation, the one who manages his life well walks the land without having to dodge the rhinoceros or the tiger. The rhinoceros finds no place for its horn, "nor the tiger a place in which to fix its claws," nor the weapon a place for its point. Then the chapter asks why, and answers: "Because there is in him no place of death." Third, what that might mean. Some readers take it close to the letter, as a picture of a charmed life. Others hear it as a map of the inside. Claws need a handhold. Insult needs pride to wound. Fear needs something we're gripping too tightly. Greed needs a hunger to hook. Where there's less clutching, there's less to catch. Fourth, closer in. A sharp email lands. A comment stings in a meeting. Notice where it bites. It may be the spot that was already sore, the reputation you're guarding, the point you need to win. The chapter makes no promise that hard things won't come. It points at the handhold, the place the claws were going to grab, and suggests there could be less of it.
screen: `CLUTCHING AT LIFE IS ITS OWN DANGER.` · `THE TIGER FINDS NO PLACE FOR ITS CLAWS.` · `CLAWS NEED A HANDHOLD.` · `WHERE THE SHARP EMAIL BITES.` · then, large: `NO PLACE OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet one danger calmly. Sit comfortably and let your breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one small danger on your horizon: a hard conversation, a bill, a result you're waiting for. Don't run from it, and don't wrestle it. Just notice where it grips. The jaw, the stomach, a story about what it will say about you. Find the handhold. Then, on an out-breath, let that spot loosen a little. If the worry comes back, meet it the same way, calmly, again. The bell holds the time.
No place for the tiger. Chapter fifty's traveler: the tiger finds nowhere to fix its claws, because there is no place of death in him. Today's word.
screen: `NO PLACE FOR THE TIGER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: no place for claws. When something sharp comes at you today, ask what it's trying to grab, and loosen your grip on that one thing. Day one thousand one hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter fifty in more than one way: some as a picture of the sage's protected life, others as a teaching that less clutching leaves less for harm to grip.

notes: Editor pass: cut the unsupported 'almost always' claim about where criticism bites, replaced the relative (used on day 1111) with a meeting comment, and replaced the recurring 'an ordinary Tuesday' turn.

The chapter's opening counts (three in ten, etc.) were deliberately left out; the opening is paraphrased as 'some hurry toward death by straining too hard to keep living.' Confirm the paraphrase is fair to Legge's 'excessive endeavours to perpetuate life.'
The inner reading (insult needs pride, fear needs gripping) is offered as what 'others' hear, not as the text's own claim. Confirm the framing.
